articles.title: Op-Ed: Bremerton Should Fully Pedestrianize Quincy Square
articles.author: Travis Merrigan
paras: The City of Bremerton is debating how to use the newly completed, $4 million Quincy Square, located at the heart of downtown. As with Seattle’s Pike Place Market, Bremerton Public Works proposed closing the ‘Q Square’ about half the days of the year. At a Sept 3rd City Council meeting, councilors were split 3-to-3 between supporting the 182-day closure and seeking more car-access days. It’s just the latest debate in an on-going tug of war as the city tries to carve out safe multimodal spaces from Bremerton’s thoroughly car-dominated streets and neighborhoods.

Completed in 2025, Quincy Square is a half-block of 4th Street in the heart of downtown. It features a permanent stage, seating and tables, and interactive music installations honoring the late, great music impresario Quincy Jones, who spent his middle school years in Bremerton, before moving to Seattle.

Q Square was designed as a hybrid street, transforming via mid-block, removable bollards between pedestrian-oriented plaza and a one-way street with 14 parking spots. The debate this fall at Bremerton City Council is about how many days the plaza should be open to cars.

The Public Works plan attempts to split the baby, via middle-of-the-road Resolution No. 3417. The resolution would change Bremerton city code to create ‘pedestrian mall’, under a little used Washington state law from the 1960s. On September 3, City Council voted 5-1 to create a pedestrian mall, but a major rift formed over whether Q Square should be primarily a pedestrian street closed to cars or just a regular street which closes sometimes for events.

Public Works’ initial proposal offered a vision of Quincy Square offering economic, safety and social benefits of a predictable schedule and community gathering space. It also cited the costs of the current, on-again off-again street closures, including resource drain and overtime required to replace signage and bollards at odd hours. The administration’s plan also cited confused drivers, forced into awkward u-turns on a street that might be open the day before.

Public Works is seeking guidance on a separate, administrative decision, to set the calendar which designates which days Q Square is open to traffic. The initial proposal was for about 182 days closed, concentrated in the summer and between Thanksgiving and New Years, with the plaza open to traffic the other 183 days.

During its September 3rd deliberations, Council was split 3-3 (with one councilmember absent) between closing Q Square to cars for at least 182-days per year, and three councilors who sought more car-access days.

Opponents of more pedestrianization of Q Square have understandable and sincere concerns about the downsides of closing the street. People who park or drive on the street are being asked to shoulder a disproportionate burden of an amenity that benefits the entire city.
Those opposing more pedestrianization of Q Square have three primary complaints:

Every multimodal project that restricts automobile access faces backlash from those who would otherwise have unfettered usage of a given space. Q Square is home to four dozen businesses, including a theater, corner store, skate shop and over 30 professional offices in a mid-rise tower. For those people, it’s more convenient to get dropped off right in front of the door than walk from a parking garage or street parking 200 feet away.

And opponents argue that, with the exception of City-sponsored events, the Square is little-used. That too few people - or the wrong kinds of people (e.g., unhoused) - hang out in the Square to justify the loss of parking and car traffic. This echoes a common criticism of ‘empty’ bike lanes; if somebody isn’t constantly in them, the space should be available for cars.

Bremerton must decide if the creation of a central, community gathering space is worth forcing inconvenience on a few dozen drivers every day. This half block of 4th St is probably downtown’s lowest-traffic street, and the 14 parking stalls are just 0.2% of downtown’s 6,300 public parking spaces. And many city amenities - parks, free street parking, park benches, and schools - sit empty most hours of the year. These amenities are valuable because they are available when needed. Nobody tears down a church because it’s empty on a Tuesday afternoon.

The status quo of random 4th Street closures leads to confused motorists making awkward half-block u-turns on a street not fit for purpose. The street could be reconfigured as a u-shaped drop-off site for cars and shuttle buses, with short-term, off-hour parking for deliveries. Resolution 3417 allows acquisition of right of way, and the affected hotel would likely welcome an improvement to the chaotic turn-arounds.

Leaving Q Square closed for long blocks of time allows drivers and businesses to adjust and find new hacks to efficiently navigate and do commerce downtown. Meanwhile, designating Q Square for pedestrians will, over time, attract more people downtown, and delight visitors who stumble across the open space.

Great cities have great plazas. Plazas are where poems are written, friends meet for lunch and kids first learn to ride bikes. The $4 million Quincy Square is brand new and, if left open for people to gather, will become the beating heart of thriving downtown Bremerton. Q Square will help downtown recover from the suburban flight of the 80s and 90s which pulled commerce out of the city, off to distant strip malls outside the city.

In modern-day Bremerton, virtually every inch of downtown street is maximized for vehicles. Among downtown’s 6,300 public parking spots are four, city-owned, multistory parking garages. Most downtown streets host two-way traffic plus dual-side on-street parking. Pedestrians are shunted aside onto narrow sidewalks, with few benches to sit on or places to linger. Street eateries that granted street life to downtown during the pandemic are nearly all swept away, to make room for street parking. The nearest playground swing is 0.75 miles away.

Revitalization of downtown requires people to get out of their cars, window shop and spend money in downtown businesses. A lovely, welcoming square that encourages people to linger will benefit many businesses downtown, even if the lost parking affects some more than others.

Bremerton could take action to reduce the hyperlocal problems caused by vehicle restrictions. Additional short-term and ADA parking could be created very near Q Square. The City could designate the four Pacific Avenue parking stalls nearest Q Square as ADA and place 2-hour parking limits on the bottom two floors of its 4th and Washington parking garage. Also, an improved turn-around and drop-off spot could be created in collaboration with the hotel immediately east of the half-block vehicle barriers.

More people would use Q Square if the city offered very low-cost rental of the space for bike polo matches, band rehearsals and mass outdoor Dungeons and Dragons tournaments (Bremerton’s nerd game is strong). The burden of filling the square need not fall on the City funding big events.

Opponents of closing Q Square predict terrible outcomes. But outcomes will probably be less dire than they predict, especially if Bremerton makes adjustments. Besides, unexpected upsides are just as likely as miserable downsides. Cities have always thrived because of spontaneous interaction in public places, which sparks ideas, creates new commerce and builds community. Q Square is unique in all of Bremerton, but common across the world: a safe, inviting, central plaza where people go just because, and where interesting and unexpected things can happen.
Great cities have great plazas. Quincy Square is Bremerton’s once-in-a-generation shot to create Bremerton’s first great plaza. Let’s not throw away our shot.
The Bremerton City Council will debate the Mayor’s proposal at an upcoming council meeting this fall.

articles.title: The Roundup: Route 7 or RapidRide? Zahilay Weighs In
paras: Last week , we talked about potential changes to bus Route 7.
We got plenty of feedback from concerned community members, so I wanted to do a follow-up.
This week, I interviewed King County Executive Girmay Zahilay.
We spoke about the proposed changes to Route 7, the feedback the Emerald has heard from the community, and the current status of the proposal.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
MD: After running our article last week, we've heard plenty of feedback from the community. What are your thoughts on the proposed changes? Do you support changing Route 7 to RapidRide R?

GZ: I definitely support RapidRide R and upgrading Route 7 because I think the South Seattle community deserves an upgrade, deserves the best possible transit service and the better overall rider experience that RapidRide brings. I think there's a lot of work to do to make sure that we're incorporating community feedback and being as accessible to all of our communities as possible. And so I want to continue working with our community to make this the best possible investment for the neighborhoods that I grew up in and care about.
MD: A question that keeps coming up is why we can't have both Route 7 and the RapidRide. Why does it have to be either or?

GZ: I think in a universe where we had unlimited resources, maybe it could be. But when you take finite resources and divide them between two projects, two different sets of buses, two different operators, two different systems that could end up with us having less of both, I don't think that's something anybody wants. And they might also interfere with each other. You know, the benefits of RapidRide are the reliability, the frequency, and having a local bus that is competing with that bus lane could present problems too.

MD: I get that. But what I'm hearing from the community is concern over the loss of 20 stops in our neighborhood. That makes it feel like a shift toward a commuter bus for getting downtown that will replace a route that has traditionally been a lifeline for people in the community traveling within the South End. A lot of people say this will make daily life harder. So I ask: Who does this serve? Is it primarily for people commuting to work downtown?

GZ: It can and should serve everyone. No one should be left behind. Not our seniors. Not people with disabilities. Not people who want local access. And not commuters. And that is a conversation that's ongoing to make sure that it does serve all of our communities.

I would not be supporting this if I didn't think it was going to be a better experience for everyone. A RapidRide R is going to have more dependable buses. It's going to have safer ways to reach the bus because of all of the infrastructure improvements that come with RapidRide. We know that a lot of parts of Rainier are treacherous, and so the better lighting, better sidewalks, better access is something that's going to be better for everyone. We're going to have more comfortable places to sit and wait. We're going to have signals that tell people when the bus is coming. The bus timing between each bus is going to be more reliable because it's going to be managed through a better system.

And, in terms of stop consolidation, I definitely hear people are wanting to preserve stops that they rely on. And because of that feedback, we've already added back in a couple of stops to the updated proposal , and I want to continue hearing from people.

I would also note that the stop consolidation piece really resonates with me, and that's why we've taken certain actions, and then we will continue to take actions. But the kind of blanket Route 7 romanticization that is happening is also not fair or accurate, in my view. You know, this is the route that I grew up taking, and until this RapidRide conversation started happening, it wasn't this kind of blanket romanticizing that was happening. Route 7 has had its fair share of issues.

MD: I also grew up taking the 7 and agree it has its issues. But I know there are still a lot of people who depend on it, many of whom have reached out with concerns about the proposals, and I know plenty of people who've voiced these concerns since 2019. It would be great to be able to communicate to them that they can have their voices heard.

GZ: Mike, can I ask you a question? When people are reaching out, are they telling you which specific stops that they are most concerned about, or are they giving you a vague concern about RapidRide in general? Because the people who are reaching out are not telling us specific stops. So the more they can tell you specific stops, the more we can be helpful.

MD: Our reporter Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero recently did a ride-along with a few community orgs and neighbors who pointed out the stops that would potentially be eliminated. She said people mentioned stops by schools and pharmacies.

GZ: Maybe that refers to Franklin. One of the stops we're adding back is on Rainier and Bayview near Mount Baker Station. Another one is on Rainier and Grand near Judkins Park Station. But again, the sense that I've been getting is that people, when they hear the number, you know, 20 stops being consolidated, that number, understandably, is making people feel like it's not going to be as accessible as it used to be. But I would really, really encourage people to sit with the map and see which ones are going to affect their lives most consequentially and then share that with us.

I think this is going to be a massive improvement for South Seattle. It's going to also be better connected to the light rail network. Right now, the 7 doesn't connect directly to the Rainier Beach Station, and the RapidRide is going to be better connected to Rainier Beach Station, Judkins Park Station, the International District, Mount Baker, and all of the downtown stations.
MD: Where exactly do we stand in this process? What are the next steps, and for the people who still want their voice to be heard before a final decision is made, how can they do so?

GZ: Today, I'm going to be transferring the alignment ordinance to the King County Council. That's going to be the ordinance that shows the stops for the RapidRide, and the Council continues to have the authority to review and add stops back in. So I would encourage the community to find out the King County Council's review schedule through the TrEE Committee — Transportation, Economy, and Environment Committee — come and testify and share again the specific stops that you're most concerned about.

Also, Metro will continue to have more community forums as we continue the design process of RapidRide, and there is a specific segment of the 7 that's going to experience the most consolidation, and those are what's called the Prentice Loop south of Henderson, and for those communities south of Henderson, Metro and myself will do a separate service process to make sure that we don't leave that community behind and make sure that they have the options that they need to connect to our transit networks, and that's going to be a commitment from me and Metro to make sure that we continue serving that community.

paras: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power. Introduction by Luke Kennard

I have an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress.

On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”. Men were portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Bee AI devices have a bystander problem, says former AWS security engineer
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon’s new Bee AI devices ask the wrong person for consent, according to a privacy and security veteran who previously worked as a senior principal security engineer at Amazon Web Services.
In a LinkedIn article , Jeff Williams writes that Bee’s consent safeguards are aimed at the wearer, while the people being recorded have no practical way to say no.

Amazon unveiled the devices Thursday , the first new Bee hardware since it acquired the San Francisco startup last year. The $74.99 Bee Frontier goes on the wrist or clips to clothing, and the $99.99 Bee Eclipse snaps onto the back of a phone.
Both turn conversations into summaries and to-do lists, with connections to Amazon.com and Alexa+ for paid subscribers.
How Bee handles consent: Amazon says users are prompted to get permission from call participants each time they start a recording, and the devices show an indicator light while in use.

The problem, Williams says, is that neither one reliably tells the other people in a conversation that they’re being recorded. He writes that the prompt appears only on the wearer’s phone, and nothing enforces it.
“A prompt instructing the user to obtain permission is a liability allocation,” he wrote, arguing that Amazon is shifting responsibility for obtaining consent onto the wearer.
The light is easy to hide under a sleeve or in a pocket, he notes, and a device on the wrist or phone sits outside the frame on a video call.

Williams points to Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses as an example. In September, the data protection authority in Hamburg , Germany, found the glasses’ recording light hard to see outdoors and concluded that a recording indicator alone doesn’t establish informed consent under Europe’s GDPR.
In the U.S., about a dozen states, including Washington state and California, generally require consent from everyone before a private conversation can be recorded.

Whose data is protected: Williams gives Amazon credit for Bee Private Compute, which processes audio in an isolated, encrypted environment built on AWS Nitro and then deletes it. Amazon says only the customer can access the resulting data, not Amazon or Bee.

But that protects the wearer. The words of the people around the wearer still end up in transcripts and summaries they can’t see or remove. Amazon says those speakers aren’t identified by name unless they complete a voice training exercise with the device’s owner.
Williams notes that Amazon has changed comparable privacy commitments before, such as ending the “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” option on some Echo devices last year.

Williams also advises companies to keep the devices out of client meetings and privileged discussions, since the transcripts end up in an employee’s personal account, where the company can’t see or manage them.

A proposed fix: Williams says Bee should leave other people’s voices out of transcripts by default, unless they’ve enrolled their voices and agreed to be recorded. Before the acquisition, Bee indicated plans to record only the voices of people who had verbally consented, according to TechCrunch .
“I know first-hand that Amazon has the engineering talent to ship it,” he wrote.
Amazon’s response: The company didn’t comment directly on the critique but pointed to safeguards built into the devices.

One is an automatic shutoff: the devices turn off if they don’t detect the owner’s voice for 5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes, depending on the user’s setting. Amazon says that reinforces that Bee is “a personal AI assistant, not a device designed to passively pick up audio throughout the day.”

The company says it educates customers about responsible use in the Bee app, and that Eclipse will send push notifications encouraging users to let people around them know they’re using Bee and to ask for permission.

Williams, now chief information security officer at Sigma360, worked at AWS from 2023 to 2025 and spent more than 12 years at Microsoft before that, including as a privacy officer for its services business. Read his full article on LinkedIn. Read his full article on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: The colorful and cranky language of the AI era, from slop to slap
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: We’ve all encountered the phrase AI slop, but what’s an AI slap ? A meat proxy? Chatfishing? Or agentsomnia? Following up on my glossary of AI , which demystified AI jargon, Prof. Dan Weld is joining me to shine a light on the nontechnical lingo of the AI era. We also sneak in a few phrases that should exist to capture the AI zeitgeist, circa 2026.
We introduce more than 35 phrases, so we’ve divided them into sections to keep the broligarchy from crowding enshittification.

“Digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence,” which is how Merriam-Webster defined slop, its 2025 word of the year. Shrimp Jesus is the specimen, Christ fused with crustaceans, posted to Facebook by the thousands.
AI cream is our name for the rare opposite, superb writing authored with the help of AI. We hope that over time the cream will rise to the top and the slop will sink.

Until that happens, we have the meat proxy , “a person who forwards AI-generated text, code, or other output without reading, understanding, or validating it.” We call the action of sending AI-generated text blindly an AI slap . It stings.

Your AI Slop Bores Me is a website where you type a prompt and a randomly chosen human answers it while pretending to be a chatbot. Fifty million views in a week , which tells you how badly people wanted to say something back.
AI suspicion is our name for the nagging feeling that what you’re reading was AI generated. You could also call it Turing tingle or AI-dar .

AI shaming is the accusation that follows, attacking someone’s work by insinuating a machine wrote it. The paper that named it is subtitled “Birth of a Classist Slur in Knowledge Work,” and it argues that the accusations fall hardest on racial minorities and on writers whose first language isn’t English.
See also: tasteslop , workslop , slopaganda .

A video or recording altered by machine learning so that a real person appears to say or do something they never said or did. Named in late 2017 for the Reddit user who called himself deepfakes. The word we all use for AI deception descends from one anonymous pornographer’s handle.
The liar’s dividend is the payoff a real wrongdoer collects once any authentic recording can be waved off as a fake. The damage isn’t the fake video. It’s that real video stops counting.

Counterfeit people was Daniel Dennett’s last argument, that machines able to pass as human are “the most dangerous artifacts in human history, capable of destroying not just economies but human freedom itself.” He wanted them outlawed and watermarked like banknotes.

Tilly Norwood is one of them, an AI actress unveiled at the Zurich Film Festival in September 2025. Her makers said talent agents wanted to sign her. Emily Blunt, shown a picture, said “Good Lord, we’re screwed” and told the agencies to stop.

Most of the damage doesn’t need AI at all. A cheapfake is manipulation made with cheap software or none at all. Chatfishing is using AI to write your messages on a dating app, where the con used to be a fake photo and is now a rented personality.

A name for the Silicon Valley billionaires and venture capitalists who think democracy is finished and want corporate rule in its place. Gil Durán’s book, subtitled Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, traces the idea to a 1997 book, The Sovereign Individual, and to Peter Thiel’s circle, which Durán says believes “technology means democracy is an obsolete software system.”
Durán didn’t coin the phrase. Someone in the crypto world told him they’d been using it for years.

Durán’s target is the broligarchy , “a small group of extremely wealthy men, particularly those in technology, who wield significant political and economic power.” The word sat on Twitter from 2009 and went nowhere until Carole Cadwalladr wrote about “a new super-class of broligarchs” in July 2024.

The mental deterioration that comes from consuming too much junk online, chosen by Oxford University Press as its 2024 word of the year. Thoreau got there first, in Walden in 1854, complaining that England was busy curing the potato-rot while nobody was curing the brain-rot.

Dead internet theory is the supply side, “a theory that a lot of the internet is no longer created by real people but rather by bots and other AI tools.” It started as a forum post in January 2021 and is quietly turning into a description.

Enshittification is Cory Doctorow’s three-stage decay: “first, they are good to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers; finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves.”

AI fatigue is what’s left over, “the exhaustion or the sense of being overwhelmed by the rapid proliferation and constant engagement with artificial intelligence technologies.” The phrase has been drifting through the trade press since 2023 with no author attached; the definition above comes from Route Fifty, a trade publication for state and local government.

Andrej Karpathy’s February 2025 coinage, crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2025, is “fully giving in to the vibes, embrac[ing] exponentials, and forget[ting] that the code even exists”—accepting whatever diff the AI hands you without reading it.

Promptatory is our word, styled on “purgatory,” for the state of being trapped in an unending edit-and-re-prompt loop with an AI system. You fix the bug the AI introduced, and in fixing it, the AI introduces two more, each smaller and more absurd than the last. Progress is hard earned: you close in on “done” like the runner in Zeno’s paradox, forever eating the remaining distance in half. Promptatory is vibe coding’s hangover: the vibe wears off, and the rereading begins.

A related condition we dub agentsomnia is the chronic inability to rest or disconnect from work, driven by the haunting feeling that your autonomous software or AI agents are stalled without your feedback. The Wall Street Journal calls it agent FOMO .

An OpenAI rallying cry. AGI is the point where a machine can do any intellectual task a person can, and the phrase became a general exclamation for the moment a model does something that rearranges your sense of what’s coming. Ilya Sutskever used it inside the company and posted it publicly in 2022. It works as celebration and as diagnosis.

P(doom) runs in the other direction: “your personal probability that AI ends the world, stated as a number so the vibe feels like math.” It started as shorthand among a small online community in 2022 and now gets asked at dinner parties.
Talk that outruns the technology comes in other flavors too.

Bragawatts , a unit of measurement for boasting, is “the practice of AI companies boasting about very large projects to create excitement and attract investment, even though many of these projects are never completed,” as Britain’s Cambridge Dictionary put it in January 2026.

Vibe revenue does the same thing to the income statement, “money or funding that an AI company is given because people are excited about the potential of AI, rather than because the company’s products are already successful.”

A one-sided relationship with someone who doesn’t know you exist. Donald Horton and Richard Wohl coined it in 1956 about television viewers, and Britain’s Cambridge Dictionary made it the 2025 word of the year , citing celebrities, influencers, and chatbots. A seventy-year-old term about Ed Sullivan turns out to describe your relationship with ChatGPT.

AI addiction is what happens when the one-sided relationship takes over. A 2026 study sorted it into three kinds: escapist roleplay, where people come to prefer the world the chatbot builds; pseudosocial companionship, where it replaces the relationships; and the epistemic rabbit hole, compulsive question-asking that crowds out everything else.
The researchers blame the design and call the chatbot an AI genie, a thing that gives you exactly anything you want with minimal effort.

AI psychosis is the far end, “a phenomenon wherein individuals reportedly develop or experience worsening psychosis, such as paranoia and delusions, in connection with their use of chatbots.” The Danish psychiatrist Søren Dinesen Østergaard suggested the term in a 2023 editorial in the journal Schizophrenia Bulletin. It isn’t a recognized clinical diagnosis, and we should say so.

Nearly every phrase above names a problem. Slop, shaming, deepfakes, brain rot, psychosis: what the AI era has added to English so far is a vocabulary of complaint. There’s still no common word for AI doing something well. We’ve offered AI cream. If you have a candidate for a phrase we’re missing, please send it to us.

articles.title: Traffic data pioneer Inrix to be acquired by Allstate’s Arity after more than two decades
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Inrix, the Bellevue, Wash.-based traffic data company that spun out of Microsoft in 2004 and became one of the Seattle region’s longest-running independent tech companies, has agreed to sell substantially all of its assets to Arity, the mobility data subsidiary of insurance giant Allstate.

The deal, announced Friday, would end Inrix ‘s 22-year run as a standalone company. Inrix has raised more than $288 million and flirted with an IPO multiple times over its lifetime. Terms were not disclosed. The companies expect the acquisition to close later this year.

Founded in 2016, Chicago-based Arity analyzes driving behavior for insurers, marketers and public-sector customers. It says it has amassed more than 3 trillion miles of driving data. The acquisition would pair that information with Inrix’s analytics on traffic, road conditions and transportation networks.

“By combining Arity’s predictive insights on driving behavior and risk with Inrix’s transportation intelligence and mobility analytics, we will be uniquely positioned to deliver more robust intelligence and insights into how people, vehicles, goods, and roads interact,” Gary Hallgren, president of Arity, said in a statement .

While the companies are touting the benefits of combining their data and analytics, Arity’s data practices have faced legal scrutiny. In January 2025, Texas sued Allstate and Arity, alleging they collected and sold consumers’ driving and location data without adequate consent. Responding to a separate consumer privacy lawsuit in March, Allstate told Reuters that users receive clear notice and explicitly opt in to sharing their driving data.

The proposed acquisition charts an alternate course to Inrix’s earlier plans for going public. In 2012 , Inrix hired Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase with an eye toward a 2013 IPO that was expected to raise up to $100 million. The company looked to go public again in 2022 but backed out amid economic uncertainty stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and other factors.

“We were about two weeks away from filing our documents with the SEC,” Inrix CEO Bryan Mistele said in an August 2022 GeekWire story . “We’re on standby right now, waiting to see when the markets and economy improve, in which case we’ll take another run at it.”
Inrix serves corporate, automotive, technology and public-sector customers including Amazon, IBM, General Motors, Windermere Real Estate and state departments of transportation.

The company got its start selling traffic and transportation-related data. In recent years, it moved beyond supplying raw traffic data into subscription software that helps customers interpret it, including tools for traffic-signal timing, road safety and retail site selection.
Recent public releases include its first Parking Scorecard, which ranks the availability and cost of parking in major cities in the U.S. and Europe.
Inrix has about 277 employees, based on LinkedIn data. The companies did not say whether all of them would remain or whether Inrix would keep its Bellevue headquarters.
The story will be updated with additional information as it becomes available.

articles.title: Retro tech meets modern AI: Inside an Amazon developer’s garage turned working computer museum
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Darko Mesaros used to park a car in the garage of his Maple Valley, Wash., home. These days, it’s wall-to-wall computers.
A towering server rack glows with red LEDs. CRT monitors are stacked beside vintage workstations, and a workbench overflows with tools, cables, and half-repaired components.

“I started getting stuff, and then … it just kind of snowballed to a point I actually had to slow down because I legitimately don’t have space for it anymore,” Mesaros told GeekWire during a recent tour of his retro hardware labyrinth.

The lore of tech innovation is full of suburban garages where visionary founders tinkered their way to world-changing companies. Mesaros, a distinguished developer advocate at Amazon Web Services, isn’t launching a startup out of his. Instead, he’s using it as a living museum to rescue, repair, and resurrect the discarded digital ghosts of computing history — and then daring them to run modern artificial intelligence.

The collection has spilled into an upstairs office and now spans more than 100 full computers, from an early-1970s minicomputer to Silicon Graphics workstations from the ’90s and HP workstations from the 2000s. Add roughly 25 vintage video game consoles, rescued software, peripherals, a leather-bound TRS-80 owner’s manual, and nearly a decade of 1980s Byte magazines, and the total tops 1,000 items.
Most of it arrives broken, and that’s the point.
“Buying a mint old system is not fun,” he said. “Buying something that’s broken and then having that excitement of fixing it is just fantastic.”

He finds gear at Goodwill, through local Facebook Marketplace groups, and through Seattle’s large retro computing community. Sometimes it takes a rescue mission: when a man in Washington, D.C., was about to throw away a pallet of 1980s computers, Mesaros had a friend there grab it, then paid to ship the whole load to Seattle.
At one point, he had seven Commodore 64s. He gives extras to other collectors, and he’s never sold a single piece.
Mesaros’ fascination with vintage hardware goes beyond nostalgia; it’s the foundation of a lifelong obsession with how things work under the hood.

Growing up in Serbia, he faced an economic reality where cutting-edge tech was out of reach. From 1991 to 2003, his only computer was a Commodore 64 — a machine released in 1982. While the rest of the computing world sped through the 1990s and early 2000s, Mesaros skipped straight to modern PCs.
“I feel like I missed that whole thing,” he said. “I missed the whole, you know, Sun workstation, Silicon Graphics, HP 9000, all of those things … and I just wanted to explore how that was.”
So he bought a couple of Sun workstations to see what he’d missed. Then he kept going.
“It’s a hobby, but it’s also a problem,” he said with a laugh.
If the garage caught fire, the one machine he’d grab? A bright blue Silicon Graphics Indy, the 1990s workstation from the very era he missed growing up. It was the first SGI he bought.
“It showed me how this amazing workstation worked!” he said. He still fires it up from time to time just to enjoy its IRIX operating system.
Still on his wish list: a DEC VT520 terminal with an amber screen. Working units only seem to turn up on the East Coast, and he won’t risk shipping a fragile CRT across the country.

Before joining Amazon nearly a decade ago, he held system administration and engineering roles at companies including AT&T and Tipico. Now at AWS, his day job involves leveraging his experience to help developers and customers adopt and use AWS services via blogs, webinars, code, and technical advocacy. The garage doubles as his set: he records AWS videos and live streams there.

Mesaros moved to the Seattle area around the start of the pandemic, arriving with a couple of workstations, a monitor, and a handful of laptops before his collection expanded. He soon realized gear was far cheaper here than in Europe.

“Most of these things are older than me. Especially older than my tech career,” the 38-year-old noted. “Actually, all of these things are older than my career. However, again, I find it fascinating how computer history has evolved.”

His arrival timing meant he narrowly missed the chance to visit Seattle’s beloved Living Computers: Museum + Labs before it permanently closed its doors . But in his own home, he’s essentially built a private version of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s former institution.
Beyond the vintage hardware, Mesaros’ appreciation for computing history is permanently etched onto his body.

He sports a collection of retro tech tattoos on his arms, including symmetrical DOS and Linux terminal prompts (C:\WINDOWS> and root@localhost), a classic Windows 95 logo, MS-DOS branding, a shebang and a quit command that mark the start and end of a script, and detailed microprocessors like the Zilog Z80 and MOS 6502 paired with assembly code — a setup he jokingly calls his literal “ARM CPUs.” He’s still waiting, he said, on his check from Microsoft.

“I only tattoo ancient technology on myself,” Mesaros said, noting that people frequently stop him at airports to take pictures. “Old technology will stay with me … I feel like this is an investment in my career.”
He has plans for more ink during his next trip home to Serbia.

For Mesaros, collecting vintage computers is about more than admiring silent plastic shells on a shelf; it’s about making them talk across the digital chasm. In his garage and upstairs office, he routinely bends ancient hardware to modern purposes — proving that an 8-bit machine or a mechanical teletype can still interface with the cutting-edge cloud.

Mesaros has chatted with an AI coding agent from a Commodore 64 and deployed Kubernetes via a 1986 Tandy 102 portable computer. He wired a 1984 DEC DECwriter IV teletype to Amazon’s Kiro coding agent, explaining in a blog post how he talks to Kiro through the clacking machine — and he’s even deployed AWS infrastructure from it.
“Should this be done? Probably not,” he said. “But is it fun? Absolutely.”

In a demo for GeekWire, we watched the teletype clatter out the agent’s answer to his query, “What is GeekWire?” After a few seconds of hammering, it printed: “Seattle-based tech news site covering Pacific Northwest startups, Amazon, Microsoft and the broader tech industry.”
Not bad for a machine older than its operator.
Mesaros also spent a weekend trying to get stuck in 1999, using a Windows 98 machine as his only computer and documenting it on a VHS camcorder.
“The only window into the future was Kiro,” he said.

While these stunts might sound like elaborate practical jokes, Mesaros believes they serve a vital purpose in the age of AI. In a modern development landscape where tools let programmers “build a to-do app and walk away,” he argues that developers are losing the art of paying attention.

He likes to point out that a 2017 Google paper titled “Attention Is All You Need” helped kick off today’s LLM boom. “Now in 2026, to be a really successful developer,” he said, “attention is all you need.”

“I think being curious and paying attention are the two most important skills for a developer these days because it is so easy not to do those things,” Mesaros said. “And if you want to be relevant, if you want to be good at your job, especially with AI, I think those are the two important things that are critical.”

When he isn’t troubleshooting an obscure serial card data-ready pin or attempting to hook up a military field phone from his native Serbia to an LLM, he balances his digital obsession with analog pursuits. He wrenches on an old Jeep TJ — parked in the driveway because there’s no room in the garage.
He’s not the only tinkerer in the house. His wife is a fashion designer who 3D prints clothing and purses on a farm of printers in one of the upstairs rooms.
“She’s more creative than I am,” he said. “I get to tinker with old things that don’t want to work, and she uses technology to actually make new things.”

When it comes to the tech he lets into his own life, Mesaros is choosy. He wears a classic analog Timex and bought Meta’s smart glasses when they came out — then sold them within a month. “I don’t like the camera on my face,” he said. (He does use a camera-free pair that can display real-time translated subtitles when he travels abroad.)

That same instinct is why he doesn’t see screens going away, even as AI agents take on more work. “We still have the need for control,” he said. “Being able to observe and see, visualize what’s happening is still important.”

articles.title: How ICE Continues to Wield Washington's Own Data
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: In the wake of accelerated immigration enforcement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) across the country this summer and into fall, new data shows that Washington state driver data is still being used to enable and assist in these arrests.

The update comes from the University of Washington Center of Human Rights (UWCHR), which published an initial report at the beginning of the year showing how Washington state driver data was being accessed to assist in federal immigration enforcement. Now, nine months later, UWCHR has data showing this practice has continued unabated. Researchers have confirmed 356 arrest incidents between August 1, 2025 and October 13, 2026 that have resulted from federal agents receiving Washington State Department of Licensing (DOL) driver data through the interstate querying system Nlets.

“We know that 356 is likely only a small fraction of the total cases that are happening,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy at a press conference on Tuesday. “Those are just the ones where we were able to confirm it with smoking gun evidence connecting a given plate search to a known immigration arrest.”
ICE continues to access this DOL data in spite of the 2019 Keep Washington Working Act and government officials being aware of this data access pathway since at least 2018, according to the report.

Federal agents’ general operating procedure is to travel to target-rich environments where they think they might find immigrants. They ask the state for data about certain license plates via Nlets, run the registered owner names they are given via Nlets through their own databases, and then decide whether to make an arrest.

Nilu Jenks, a candidate for the District 5 seat of the Seattle City Council, wants to add the Seattle Police Department’s use of Nlets to the Office of the Inspector General’s annual surveillance review while also calling for action from the state legislature and Governor Bob Ferguson.

“In District 5, ‘target rich’ is a polite way of saying racial profiling,” said Jenks. “It means agents deciding who looks deportable by the color of their skin and the work truck they drive: the roofer outside a hardware store on Aurora, the landscaping crew in Maple Leaf, the dad dropping his kids at school in Lake City. When a license plate becomes a name and home address in moments, every trip is a risk. Nobody should have to wonder whether it's safe to drive because of how they look, and no state database should help put a target on their backs.”
Godoy underlined that Washington state hasn’t been doing enough to address the increasing levels of violence and fear experienced by immigrant residents.

“This is a time of extraordinary pain and difficulty for immigrant communities in Washington and around our country, not only because we are experiencing unprecedented levels of immigration enforcement here in the region and around the country, but also because we're experiencing the use of increasingly violent tactics, which appear to involve overt racial profiling, often warrantless arrests, which challenge the Constitution,” Godoy said. “Multiple courts around the nation have found these practices to be unconstitutional, in fact, but here in Washington, this has been greeted thus far with relative silence, which I believe contributes to the invisibilization and isolation of immigrant communities in our midst.”

Immigration enforcement has quietly increased across the country this summer, with ICE eschewing the more dramatic “surges” it conducted earlier in the year in Minneapolis, Chicago, and other cities. Washington state has been no exception to this swell, and Godoy said she expects to see the numbers continue to rise over time.
The Seattle Times reported that 74% of ICE arrests in Washington in June and July did not involve people with criminal convictions or pending charges.

Guillermo Rivera from Eastside for All, an equity advocacy organization, spoke about the detentions being observed on the Eastside at the press conference. “Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles, and this is not only happening in East King County, this is happening all around the state,” Rivera said. “The people are being detained when they are driving. People, we are afraid now to go into our cars, that they can stop us at any time. We're afraid to go to the supermarket, to take the kids to the doctor, to take our children to school.”

The UWHRC report described a common new technique being seen in ICE detentions known as “jump outs.” “Jump outs” involve multiple unmarked vehicles, sometimes lacking license plates, surrounding a target who is driving. Unidentified officers then jump out of their cars and violently detain their target. Officers often already know the name of the person they are detaining due to the state driver data they have accessed.
The “jump out” has become one of ICE’s key enforcement strategies since President Donald Trump began his second term.

19 of 22 shootings by immigration agents in Trump’s second term have taken place during these ICE traffic stops, an analysis this summer found, with the UWHRC identifying at least two additional ICE shootings during traffic stops since then.

The increasing brutality of immigration enforcement is also typified by two recent investments by ICE: up to $2 million on robot dogs and up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks.

Meanwhile, local lawmakers still don’t know if ICE is planning to buy the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, which could stymie state efforts to impose oversight on the facility. ICE’s current contract with the facility is set to expire on October 27.

The detention center has been receiving complaints about poor and dehumanizing conditions for years. Indeed, conditions there are so bad that Washington State Senator Yasmin Trudeau (D-Tacoma) refers to the facility as a concentration camp.

UW researchers found evidence that in Minnesota, driver data queries were also being used to obtain information about community observers of ICE activity, which shows how similar tactics can be used to both increase immigration detentions and to surveil U.S. citizens without a warrant.
The UWHRC also found evidence that this practice is happening right here in King County.

This past June, community member Tony Andrews saw a suspicious vehicle in a Fred Meyer parking lot in Bellevue. Andrews had attended a constitutional observer training through Indivisible Eastside, which allowed him to identify the vehicle as possibly belonging to ICE. Even though Andrews kept his distance, the suspicious vehicle circled tightly around Andrews’ car in the parking lot.

Andrews gave his vehicle information to the UW researchers who submitted a records request. The returned records showed that his license plate had been run through Nlets on the day and time that the incident with the suspicious vehicle took place.
“For me, this was just a violation of my privacy,” Andrews told The Urbanist . “For the immigrants, these violations are life-changing. For them, it can mean family separation.”
The UWHRC report detailed four different pathways by which ICE and other federal agents are able to get state driver data:
The report emphasized that all pathways must be addressed simultaneously; otherwise ICE will simply shift to a new means of accessing the data.
In Washington state, ICE had been accessing driver data via direct access to the state DMV databases as recently as last year , but for now, that pathway appears to be closed.

DOL sold its data to 14 companies last year, including at least three who held Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts in the near past. While these contracts with DOL forbid the data brokers from selling the data for immigration enforcement purposes, one of the companies, LexisNexis, has structured at least one past contract with ICE in such a way that LexisNexis would have no ability to see how ICE has been using the data. Therefore, it is impossible to be confident that ICE cannot use the data broker pathway to access Washington state driver data.
Direct agency sharing data with ICE is illegal under the Keep Washington Working Act, although that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening anyway.
However, the primary way ICE appears to be accessing DMV data in Washington state at this time is through the Nlets queries.

Governor Bob Ferguson has said that his office’s actions of canceling ICE and DHS’s access to Nlets has resulted in blocking 100,000 attempts to use Nlets to access state data. However, the UWHRC report found that from January 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, DHS-affiliated agencies still searched the DOL database via Nlets 3,696,147 times, showing the gaping hole in the state’s data protections.

“What happens is that those arrest patrols, whether they're made of ICE, of the Border Patrol, of combined agencies, or of unknown masked men, simply log in under another agency's ORI, just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” Godoy said. “As a result, between January and June 2026, Washington DOL data itself shows that over one million searches were completed of Washington driver and vehicle data by agencies who are part of DHS.”
So far UWHRC has documented 38 unique ORIs, or passwords, affiliated with federal agencies prior to arrests by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) in Washington state.

The report did find that New York State has been successful at cutting off the Nlets channel of information via robust legislation. In New York, federal agents are now only able to search out-of-state license plates via Nlets.

Pacific Rim Solidarity Network sent a statement to be read at the press conference instead of coming to speak due to fears of retaliation. They called for Ferguson to enable more transparency and accountability when it comes to DOL data sharing.

“Legislatures take time, and our communities need an answer now. We cannot wait until the next fall to have protections for Washington residents,” Rivera said. “We're asking the governor's office to act now. We're asking the governor to review how this information is being collected, how it's been shared, find any gaps or misuse, and use his authority to protect Washington residents.”

If Ferguson continues to choose not to close these documented gaps, the state legislature can act in January to make the Keep Washington Working Act more robust. Godoy emphasized that being even more explicit about the need for a court warrant in order to access state driver data wouldn’t be sufficient.

“The state has already incorporated specific requirements that Nlets comply with Keep Washington Working or face consequences, and yet has been inexplicably reticent to enforce these very agreements,” the report reads.

Accordingly, Godoy suggested adding explicit enforcement mechanisms to the Keep Washington Working Act, including a private right of action so that those harmed by the data sharing could receive restitution and potentially obtain court injunctions ordering a halt to illegal data access.

“We need to demand that Washington take action to at least protect us in the ways that it can,” Godoy said. “There's no way for Washington to just expel ICE agents from the state. That's not going to happen. But they don't need to serve us up to them on a silver platter with all of our data to make it so easy for them, to allow them to legitimate their arrests and their campaign of fear. So I think for electeds, this is your moment.”
Godoy also praised community members who have chosen to be involved in rapid response in defense of their immigrant neighbors.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Advances First Construction Project
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A new 20-unit apartment building in the Central District is set to make history as the first new development constructed by Seattle's three-year-old Social Housing Developer (SSHD). With a unanimous vote of the SSHD board to acquire a 7,800-square-foot property on E Yesler Way Thursday night, the vision of growing Seattle's housing stock with a new type of permanently affordable homes takes another major step forward.

The parcel set to be transformed into social housing, located at 2402 E Yesler Way, comes with an extra layer of meaning for Seattle housing advocates. It currently belongs to the family of former House Speaker Frank Chopp, who passed away in 2025 after a long career advocating around housing issues in the state legislature. Chopp's widow, Nancy Long, currently controls the property.

"It's very emotional because Frank was the first lawmaker that came out and supported social housing when House Our Neighbors ran the first initiative and [he] talked to multiple people on our behalf," SSHD Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy told The Urbanist following the vote. "So this is an incredible moment. I know that he would be proud, and it was really amazing that Nancy brought the property to us because she wanted it to be either affordable or social housing."
Construction is planned to start in 2027, with the building opening to tenants in 2028. The sale price for the land was $1.2 million, McCoy said, with a total project cost of $15 million.

This new project will be the SSHD's second housing project overall, ahead of what is expected to be an accelerated pace of property acquisition. Earlier this year, the developer took over operations of the 150-unit Elara at the Market along Western Avenue after purchasing that 2018 building for $60.9 million. More than 10,000 people applied for a chance to live in the first phase of rental units that were opened up to new applications this past spring.

Dedicated funding for the SSHD comes from a 5% payroll tax on annual compensation over $1 million, approved by Seattle voters in February 2025 with the passage of Proposition 1A. Annual revenues that were projected at approximately $50 million have proven extremely conservative, with $115 million coming in during the first year of collections. Those additional resources are set to allow the developer to scale up faster than previously anticipated.

McCoy, who previously served as the Co-Executive Director with House Our Neighbors, took over as Interim CEO in January after Roberto Jimenez, the first pick to lead the SSHD, was fired by the board . A key hire after Jimenez's departure was Ginger Segel, brought on as chief real estate development officer.

Central District House, as the developer is calling the E Yesler Way project, will be built to passive house standards, McCoy said. Architect and Baugruppen evangelist Michael Eliason, a past contributor to The Urbanist , remains the developer's director of design & policy.

Though details around planned design are scant right now, we do know that there are plans to approach the site a little differently than a normal market rate developer would. Thanks to a state law passed earlier this year – House Bill 1687 – social housing developers have expanded authority to request variances from existing zoning standards, authority that had previously only applied to public housing authorities.

"We are looking to utilize our new power under the Housing Cooperation Law to try to to try to move a setback so that we can be better neighbors and not have windows going directly next to the next door neighbor," McCoy said.
McCoy brought up the fact that the social housing developer's first project will be built in a neighborhood that has seen significant upheaval in its population over the past few decades.

"We also recognize the deep tension – it's in the Central District, it has a very racist past in there, and there's still massive displacement that is happening," McCoy said. "So we are excited about using a community preference plan, a really robust affirmative marketing plan, learning from folks that have done that so successfully there."

Central District House is just the start of planned property acquisitions by the Social Housing Developer, with plans advancing for work on both new build projects and acquisitions. A project pipeline that received a board vote Thursday, contingent on the issuance of bonds that will allow the payroll tax funding currently coming in to be leveraged much further, would see six new construction projects and four acquisitions move forward through the end of 2027.

"There's so much more we're doing that isn't public yet because we have to wait for our board of directors to let us talk about them," McCoy said. "I see a lot of momentum. There will be another announcement [of] between 50 and 250 units that is going to be coming in the end of the year, beginning of next year, and much more to come."

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Two RapidRide R Line Stops Restored
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On Wednesday, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay transmitted RapidRide R Line alignment legislation to the King County Council. The R Line will travel between Rainier Beach station and downtown Seattle on Rainier Ave when it opens in 2032. In August, Metro asked the public for feedback on an initial alignment proposal . While many support the project, the planned removal of several existing Route 7 stops drew widespread criticism from Rainier Valley residents , transit advocates , and disability advocates .

In response to this feedback, the latest plan restores the stops on Rainier at Bayview St and State St/Grand St. The King County Council will discuss and vote on the R Line’s alignment over the next few weeks. This will establish the route’s path and general station locations. Additional project components, such as transit priority infrastructure, new crossings, and sidewalk improvements, will be finalized in later project stages. Executive Zahilay has proposed front-loading the project’s budget in an effort to potentially move up the R Line’s opening date.

Another key feedback theme Metro received involved the removal of stops along the Prentice Street loop. Today, every third Route 7 bus continues south of Henderson St to provide coverage in Rainier Beach. The R Line will turn right on to Henderson and terminate at the Rainier Beach Link station. In response, Metro highlighted Route 106 on Renton Ave and the Rainier Beach Metro Flex zone. The agency is also planning a southeast Seattle restructure that will take place in 2028 or 2029. Based on feedback received during restructure process, Metro may adjust other routes to back-fill Prentice St loop coverage once the R Line launches in 2032.

articles.title: Refining ramen on Capitol Hill: A decade of noodles, craft, and devotion at Ooink
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Ten years after launching their cozy Capitol Hill ramen spot above the Broadway and Pike QFC , Ooink founders Chong Boon Ooi and Jiaxin Wang are marking a decade in business.

Before establishing the shop, Malaysian-born chef Chong logged 15 years in kitchens across Los Angeles, Paris, Las Vegas, New York City, and Hawaii before choosing Seattle as the permanent home to build his craft and raise a family.

Rather than overhauling the menu to chase trends, Chong’s foundation has been meticulous refinement. As he told CHS about his culinary approach, “We still try to refine what we do and achieve better. I don’t like to create new dishes, I like to do what I do and make it better.”
The result is a noodle shop for noodle lovers. While people sometimes line up around the block for social media-driven ramen hype in the neighborhood, Ooink’s success is about devotion and longevity.

The focus has included small innovations over the years, from mala-spiced bowls to rich broths, shallot-and-goose-fat Shanghai Style Shoyu, and sourcing soft, alkaline natural spring water from a tap in Lynnwood to make his house noodles noticeably lighter and fluffier.

Ooink navigated the pandemic and industry shifts with to-go ramen kits and a hearty fried chicken sandwich, supported throughout by a devoted following. That sustained enthusiasm fueled an expansion across town, leading the team to open a second Ooink outpost at 3630 Stone Way N in Fremont.

CHS reported here on the 2016 debut of Ooink as the first-time restaurant owners were happy to take over a fully built-out space where another food and drink venture had just gone kaput. Ooink has endured, even outlasting Harvard Market ownership. Early this year, the shopping center was acquired by San Diego-based developer Tourmaline Capital for $14.2 million. Increased maintenance and more spending on security has followed and helped address some of the public safety issues on the block.
Reflecting on the decade, Ooi and Wang, have a message for Capitol HIll:

Ten years ago, we opened a tiny ramen shop above the QFC on Capitol Hill with a small menu, big dreams, and probably not enough sleep. We didn’t know how many bowls we’d serve, how many friends we’d make, or how much Seattle would become home. Ten years later, we’re still here, making noodles fresh, refining our broth, serving the ramen we believe in, and feeling incredibly grateful for every person who has slurped, sweated, waited, supported, and come back for another bowl. From our first little shop to the Ooink family today: thank you for 10 years of ramen, community, and memories.
Ooink is located at 1416 Harvard Ave. You can learn more at ooinkramen.com .

articles.title: $16.7M: Follow-up to April audit shows how King County Regional Homelessness Authority’s shortfall built over years
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Calls are growing louder to scrap the effort altogether with revelations that the King County Regional Homelessness Authority has an estimated $16.7 million “unresolved funding” shortfall on its hands and owes millions to the King County Investment Pool .
A review commissioned by the city and King County found no evidence of missing or diverted funds.

Instead, officials say the deficit stems from $15.6 million in lost administrative revenue. Under shifting local priorities and funding, and tied up in bureaucracy and process, service providers spent far less grant money than budgeted, which cut the administrative fees KCRHA was set to earn. KCRHA also spent $3.3 million beyond its funding caps on Salesforce, temporary staff, and legal fees, and racked up $2.4 million in net interest by running overdraft balances in the King County Investment Pool, a county treasury structure that manages operating funds and provides liquidity for regional public agencies.
The report (PDF) attributed the failure to weak financial management systems that failed to link budgeting, billing, and cash reconciliation.
To stabilize operations, KCRHA officials say they are rebuilding accounting controls.
In 2027, KCRHA will transfer local contract administration back to Seattle and King County, refocusing the agency on a smaller portfolio of state and federal responsibilities.

The downsizing of the authority began this summer as officials were forced to restructure the KCRHA after a troubling April 2026 forensic audit found massive deficiencies in the authority’s financial management, internal controls, and oversight.

The authority was formed as officials pledged the new effort would consolidate efforts to address the homelessness crisis at a broader, more regional level. At one point growing to a $250 million a year effort, KCRHA was officially established in late 2019 through an Interlocal Agreement between the county and the City of Seattle under then- Mayor Jenny Durkan and then- King County Executive Dow Constantine .
The King County Regional Homelessness Authority is currently led by Kelly Kinnison who has served as its Chief Executive Officer since 2024 .
The KCHRA’s budget was proposed as $205 million in 2026 with about 60% coming from Seattle and the rest from the county and state and federal pass-through grants.
Seattle is shifting its homelessness spending. Mayor Katie Wilson’s deficit-snuffing budget proposal incorporates the return of homelessness contracting to the city.

In a joint statement, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay and Wilson said the county and city are working on a repayment plan to cover the KCHRA shortfall financed on credit through King County’s treasury as the authority continues its restructuring.
Others are calling for the plug to be pulled. King County Councilmember Rod Dembowski and Seattle City Councilmember Maritza Rivera repeated calls for the authority’s dissolution.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Announces First Construction Project
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: At a chilly morning press conference today, Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD) Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy announced plans for the agency’s first original construction project, a five-story apartment building in the Central District on the lot that used to belong to the late housing advocate Rep. Frank Chopp. Scheduled to open in 2028, the development will provide 20 units of housing, leased at a mix of affordable and market rate rents.

The Central District site is SSHD’s second official housing project, following the May acquisition of the 150-unit Elara at the Market in Belltown. The two are part of a rapidly expanding housing portfolio—the agency hopes to reach 1,000 units owned or in the pipeline by the end of 2027. McCoy says the SSHD has a third yet-to-be-announced acquisition that will bring the total to 300 units by the end of this year.

The announcement comes in the midst of SSHD’s herculean expansion effort—it’s looking to nearly triple its staffing over the next 14 months. All this is funded by a surprisingly large windfall from Seattle’s social housing tax on big corporations. But to keep the momentum, the agency needs to maintain its careful balancing act to keep our fickle local politicians on its side.

Established by two ballot initiatives, SSHD operates on a model that is relatively unique for public housing in the US. Instead of only serving poor households, residents from a broad range of class backgrounds are allowed to live in social housing, with wealthier tenants subsidizing the rents of their lower income neighbors.

As part of its mission SSHD is trying to be better than your average for-profit (or even non-profit) landlord. With the Elara, SSHD provided free ORCA transit cards to all residents, froze the rent for two years, and is working to end previous landlord Greystar’s practice of distributed utility building , which divides costs equally among tenants instead of based on usage. It has also hired a restorative justice manager to address intra-tenant conflicts.

SSHD spokesperson Lilly Ana Fowler says the efforts are already yielding results, with the building’s monthly turnover rate plummeting to below 2 percent, well below the average for market rate apartments. According to Fowler, 16 new low-income renters have moved into the Elara, and the agency plans for a total of 60 units in the building to be dedicated to households making less than 50 percent of the area median income.

The agency also wants to be a top-notch developer, pledging to use union labor for its constructions and follow green passive house and universal design standards. But these efforts don’t come cheap—at a total budgeted cost of $15 million, the new Central District apartments will cost roughly $750,000 a unit.

Part of this cost is also due to the mixture of units: The majority of homes in the building will be geared toward families, with 2 or 3 bedrooms. (Less than a third of all Seattle area rentals have two or more bedrooms, according to Zillow listing data ).

But, unlike most government agencies, SSHD is working with what could be considered a bounty of resources. Its primary source of revenue—the voter-approved 5 percent corporate surcharge on salaries above $1 million—delivered $136 million in tax revenue last year and an additional $59 million in the first half of 2026. This is about two and a half times more than was expected, and has put the agency under pressure to deliver.

Earlier this year, SSHD increased its 2027 year-end production goal by 70 percent. It currently has at least six additional new projects planned for the next year. In addition to the social housing tax money and rental income, the developer plans to issue a $270 million bond to pay for the portfolio expansion.

The SSHD will have to carefully navigate the choppy waters that are Seattle politics and rebuff politicians’ innate tendency to appropriate money for their own goals. To this end, the JumpStart payroll tax serves as a cautionary parable; Once upon a time most of its revenues was supposed to go to affordable housing, but now it’s mainly used to fill the budget deficit. Seattle City Council members are already circling the SSHD’s pot of money. At a September 29 budget committee meeting, Councilmember Bob Kettle floated the idea of diverting social housing tax money for other affordable housing projects. He can’t actually do that. Not yet, at least. The two-year period in which council members are not allowed to amend the tax expires in February 2027.

Several notable political allies stood with the SSHD at the press conference, including state legislators, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and a staff member from Councilmember Dionne Foster’s office. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson did not send a representative, but she has previously shown strong support for the developer.
One notable absence was Council President Joy Hollingsworth, who represents the Central District and is rumored to be considering a mayoral run when Wilson’s term is up.

That hesitance may foreshadow a lukewarm reception to the neighborhood. The dynamics of development in the Central District are complicated and painful, with urban renewal policies displacing the majority of residents from the historic heart of Seattle’s Black community over the last 30 years. This adds a layer to the typical “NIMBY” concerns of having a new five-story building show up down the block.

At the press conference, Reverend Dr. Robert L. Jeffrey, Sr. of New Hope Missionary Baptist Church spoke supportively of the project, saying that SSHD’s community preference policy will give people with ties to the Central District “an opportunity to return home.”
“This type of initiative is what the Central District and the greater Seattle city needs,” Jeffrey said.
McCoy has indicated that SSHD will not shy away from pursuing taller developments in the future to maximize economies of scale and increase the number of people who can live in social housing.

One of the main pathways for SSHD to achieve this is by entering into housing cooperation agreements with the City, which allow it to bypass virtually all zoning requirements with a vote from the council. So to realize its ambitious goals, the SSHD will need to continue to thread the political needle.

The 7,800-square-foot Central District lot slated for development is a special case. It’s the home of former Washington State House Speaker Frank Chopp. During his time in the legislature, Chopp—who passed away last year—was a strong advocate for affordable housing. He also secured $200,000 in seed funding for the SSHD.

Chopp’s widow Nancy Long told The Stranger that due to high taxes, it didn’t make financial sense for her family to keep the property, but selling to a for-profit developer was off the table. The SSHD made a good prospective buyer, with its quick two-year development cycle, and cemented another brick in Chopp’s legacy.
“He would be very proud, I think, for this to be used for affordable housing,” Long says.
McCoy says the SSHD is talking with the City about relocating Chopp’s old blue heron-shaped tiny home and preserving it as a landmark.

Correction: An earlier version of this story stated that the agency plans for 60 units in the Elara to be dedicated to households making less that 80 percent median income. The units are for those making less than 50 percent of the area median income. We regret the error.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: 4UST Collective
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.
Is 4UST Collective Seattle’s Next Big Hip-Hop Export?

Hip-hop typically hits harder when rappers are backed by actual ace musicians, as performances by the Roots and Shabazz Palaces (among others) prove. Seattle’s fast-rising 4UST (pronounced “forest”) uphold that claim with a grip of riveting live sets and recordings such as TR4IL MIX and All About the Growf . Led by MCs Webb Wavvy, D. Mikey, and Tyler Soze, they’re a tight crew in which all of the many moving parts smoothly click into place with a satisfying inevitability: intricate vocal arrangements, strong, fluid flows, clever wordplay, and instrumentation that expresses gritty funkiness, gripping suspense, or chill bluntedness from producer Qreepz, drummer/vocalist Mr. Hendrixxx, guitarist Aaron Lusher, bassist Palmer McDaniel, and others. Sure, 4UST have plenty of songs about weed, but the lyrics are cleverer than most about its importance to the (agri)culture—e.g., “All I need is some indica and I’m in da cut” from “Potluck.” With every track and gig, 4UST refute the common belief that pot induces laziness.
